Back then, I would call my mother every Sunday.
On winter mornings my father would make coffee before anyone woke up.
We would leave the office at nine and nobody thought it was strange.
I used to be very disorganized. (a state — "would" does not work here)
Daniel, you are always up before everyone. Have you always been like that?
Not at all. Back then, I would work until midnight and sleep until nine.
What changed?
I picked up running, badly, in 2019. Nowadays I am up at six, and I stick to it even on Sundays.
You are a real creature of habit, then.
Completely. I also cut down on coffee — two cups, never after two in the afternoon.
And when do you wind down?
Nine thirty, in theory. I still skip that part when the week gets heavy.
Back then, I would work until midnight every night.
Nowadays I stop at eight and wind down before bed.
I cut down on coffee last year, and I have stuck to it.
I am a creature of habit — same route, every day.
I still skip the gym when the week gets heavy.

People ask me how I finally built a reading habit, and the honest answer is embarrassing. Back then, I would buy four books in January, read eleven pages of the first one, and feel guilty until December. Every year, the same thing. What changed was not motivation. It was size. I decided to read two pages after brushing my teeth at night. Two pages. It felt ridiculous, and that is exactly why I stuck to it. Nowadays I read about thirty minutes before bed, and it is how I wind down. I did not become a different person. I am still a creature of habit, and I still skip nights when I get home late. The difference is that skipping one night no longer ends the whole thing. If you want a habit to survive, make it so small that a bad week cannot kill it.

There are two ways to talk about the past that sound almost the same, and English speakers choose between them without noticing. Used to and would. Used to is the safe one. It works for actions, and it works for states. I used to live in Dublin. I used to be terrible at mornings. Both are fine. Would is narrower, and that is what makes it beautiful. It only works for repeated actions, and only once your listener already knows which period you are talking about. That is why a story usually opens with used to and then switches. When I was twenty-two I used to live in Dublin. Every Friday I would walk home along the canal, and I would stop at the same bakery. Notice what happened. The first sentence set the scene; the would sentences painted it. But you cannot say I would be terrible at mornings, because being terrible is not something you did on Fridays. It is a state, and states belong to used to.

First, I set the period: back then, when I was managing two teams at once. Then I paint the repeated actions with would: I would answer email until midnight, every night. After that, I name the moment something changed, like the week I picked up walking. Next, I describe the week nowadays, and I say which habit I have stuck to. In the end, I admit the one I still skip whenever the week gets heavy.
